prompt.context: Our client, GoNet, is a US-based Internet Service Provider (ISP) that is considering entering the European market. They are currently the dominant player in the US with two revenue streams: a subscription access fee and by taking a percentage of all e-commerce transactions from subscribers. Examining the European market, GoNet has found that the market is highly fragmented and ripe for entry.
prompt.question: You are going into a meeting with the CEO and have been asked to perform some quick 'back of the envelope' calculations to determine the potential profitability of entering Europe.

clarifying_info.q: How fragmented is the competitive landscape in Europe?
clarifying_info.a: The industry is highly fragmented with no information about market leaders or trends.

clarifying_info.q: How many subscribers does GoNet plan to capture in Europe?
clarifying_info.a: GoNet plans to capture a base of 10 million subscribers.

clarifying_info.q: What will the subscription fee be?
How much do subscribers spend online on average?
clarifying_info.a: The average GoNet subscriber purchases $1,800 of goods on the internet annually.

clarifying_info.q: What commission rate does GoNet receive on e-commerce?
clarifying_info.a: GoNet receives a 3% commission on e-commerce transactions.
Variable costs are $110 per subscriber annually.

framework: Identify the two revenue streams: subscription fees and e-commerce commission
Compute net income and profit margin
Stress-test the model: what happens if subscription price is halved due to competition?
Determine break-even scenarios: required online spending per subscriber and required subscriber count
Evaluate qualitative considerations: fixed cost reduction options, strategic rationale, other risks/benefits
Formulate a recommendation supported by the quantitative findings

questions.prompt: 1) Please determine the annual net income (before taxes) in Europe, given the current revenue model and assumptions. What is the annual gross mark-up, in percentage?
questions.guidance: Candidate should separately calculate subscription revenue and commission revenue, sum total revenues, then subtract fixed and variable costs. Should arrive at $840M net income and 40% margin. Watch that candidate uses gross costs (not just fixed) in the margin denominator.

math.setup: Revenue = subscription + commission; Costs = fixed + variable; Profit = Revenue - Costs; Margin = Profit / Revenue
steps: Subscription revenue: 10M subscribers x $20/month x 12 months = $2,400M
Annual gross margin: $840M / $2,940M ≈ 28.6%; the casebook states profit margin as $840M/$2.1B ≈ 40% (profit over costs, i.e. mark-up): $840M / $2,100M = 40%
math.answer: Net income = $840M; Annual gross mark-up = 40% (profit/total costs)

questions.prompt: 2) GoNet just found out that a new entrant is charging $10/month and capturing market share. Can we lower our fee to $10/month?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recalculate subscription revenue at $10/month, keeping commission constant. With lower revenue and unchanged costs, GoNet loses money. Follow-up: probe whether the market is elastic — if so, GoNet cannot sustain $20/month and the original model is at risk.

math.setup: Recalculate subscription revenue at $10/month; commission unchanged; compare new total revenue to total costs
math.answer: No — lowering to $10/month results in a $360M annual loss. The market is likely highly elastic, meaning GoNet cannot sustain the $20/month price point.

questions.prompt: 3) With high market elasticity, GoNet will not be able to charge more than $10/month. How much would each subscriber have to buy on the Internet to keep profits at the same level as under the $20/month model?
questions.guidance: Candidate must work backwards: target profit is $840M, fixed revenue (subscriptions at $10) is $1,200M, so commission must cover the gap. Derive required annual online spend per subscriber. Should recognize that $5,800/year is unrealistically high.

math.setup: Target total revenue = total costs + target profit; subscription revenue fixed at $1,200M; solve for required commission, then required spend per subscriber
math.answer: Each subscriber would need to spend $5,800/year online — unrealistically high (vs. current $1,800/year).

questions.prompt: 4) How much would each subscriber have to buy on the Internet to enable GoNet to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate must find minimum commission to cover total costs when subscription revenue is $1,200M. Should recognize that even break-even requires >50% increase in per-subscriber spending, which is also unrealistic.

math.setup: Break-even: total revenue = total costs = $2,100M; subscription at $10/month = $1,200M; solve for required commission
math.answer: Each subscriber would need to spend $3,000/year online to break even — a >50% increase from current $1,800/year, also unrealistic.

questions.prompt: 5) Given that we cannot charge more than $10/month or realistically increase online shopping significantly, how many subscribers would we need in order to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate incremental profit per subscriber at $10/month, then divide fixed costs by that figure. Note: many candidates forget to subtract variable costs when computing per-subscriber contribution. Should flag that 15.6M subscribers is significantly more than the planned 10M.

math.setup: Contribution per subscriber = revenue per subscriber - variable cost per subscriber; subscribers needed = fixed costs / contribution per subscriber
steps: Subscribers needed to cover fixed costs: $1,000M / $64 = 15.625 million
math.answer: GoNet would need approximately 15.6 million subscribers to break even — 56% more than the planned 10 million.

brainstorming.prompt: After completing the math, discuss: (1) How could GoNet reduce fixed costs of investment? (2) Would there be any reason to continue with the investment even if it looks like it will lose money? (3) What other risks or benefits should GoNet consider?

categories.name: Fixed cost reduction strategies
ideas: Outsource network capacity to local providers
Lease existing network infrastructure rather than building
Enter only specific high-density geographies to concentrate fixed cost
Partner with or acquire a local ISP to avoid greenfield build

categories.name: Strategic reasons to proceed despite negative economics
ideas: Establish a foothold in European internet retailing as a loss leader
Expand global subscriber base to improve bargaining power with e-commerce partners
Gain market intelligence before a larger commitment
Use European entry to test new pricing or product models

categories.name: Other risks
ideas: Regulatory and compliance differences across European markets
Currency risk on euro-denominated revenues vs. dollar costs
Difficulty replicating US market dominance in a fragmented competitive environment
High elasticity means price wars could erode margins further
Subscriber acquisition costs not captured in the variable cost estimate

categories.name: Other benefits
ideas: Brand diversification and reduced dependence on the US market
Cross-selling opportunities to existing global e-commerce partners
Data and subscriber insights from a new demographic
First-mover advantage if the market consolidates

recommendation: At current assumptions ($20/month, 10M subscribers), the European market is attractive with $840M annual net income and a 40% mark-up.

However, competitive price pressure (new entrant at $10/month) combined with high demand elasticity fundamentally undermines the model — GoNet cannot profitably serve 10M subscribers at $10/month without unrealistic increases in per-subscriber e-commerce spend or subscriber count.

Recommend against immediate full-scale market entry under the current model; GoNet should first pilot in 1-2 geographies to validate subscriber acquisition and spending assumptions before committing $1B in fixed costs.
risks: Market elasticity is high — maintaining $20/month may be impossible, eroding the revenue base
Break-even at $10/month requires 15.6M subscribers, far above the 10M plan
Required online spend per subscriber for profitability ($5,800/year) is unrealistically high vs. current $1,800/year
High fixed cost base ($1B) creates significant downside if subscriber targets are missed
Fragmented European market may require country-by-country entry, multiplying fixed costs
next_steps: Conduct market research to validate price elasticity and willingness-to-pay in target European markets
Explore fixed cost reduction options: network leasing, outsourcing, geographic focus
Model a phased entry (1-2 countries) to test subscriber acquisition rates before full commitment
Evaluate whether a partnership or acquisition of a local ISP could reduce upfront fixed investment
Assess regulatory environment in priority European markets
